settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: matches() already requires the whole input region to be consumed, so many simple patterns (e.g. exact '/admin') correctly reject a URL with a trailing CR/LF; a bypass requires a pattern whose wildcards exclude line terminators (typically '.').
Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE is the only flag ever used here; no DOTALL flag is set by this class, so wildcard behavior is the plain Java default and the weakness is pattern-dependent, not unconditional.

The match target is servletPath + pathInfo + queryString built from container-provided getters (lines 91-106), not raw bytes, so reachability of CR/LF depends on container decoding rather than on this class.
candidates.description: RegexRequestMatcher.matches(HttpServletRequest) builds the string to test from request.getServletPath() plus optional pathInfo and queryString (lines 91-106) and then evaluates it with pattern.matcher(url).matches() (line 113). The pattern is compiled from user/application-supplied configuration in the constructor (lines 66-72) with only optional Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE, and no \A / \z anchoring or DOTALL handling is applied. This is the same code shape that later required a security fix (the RegexRequestMatcher authorization-bypass class of issue) because Java's matches() still allows a trailing/embedded line terminator to be excluded from the match when the regex relies on '.'-based wildcards, so a request URL containing CR/LF (e.g. via %0d%0a decoding by the servlet container) can fail to match a rule that was intended to be restrictive, or match a rule that was intended to be permissive. Because RegexRequestMatcher is commonly used for security constraints (e.g. permit/deny of URL patterns), an unanchored pattern is an authorization-decision weakness. This is reported as a candidate: the repository snapshot was not instrumented and no exploit was executed, so the practical bypass depends on the specific configured regex and on the container's decoding behavior.
missing_evidence: No configured regex instances were located in the reviewed spans, so it is not shown that any deployed matcher actually uses a line-terminator-sensitive pattern.
The servlet container configuration (decoding of %0d%0a into servletPath/pathInfo) was not examined in the reviewed source.
No test or runtime evidence was read that demonstrates a concrete authorization decision flipping because of a terminator.
preconditions: Security configuration uses RegexRequestMatcher (directly, or via <intercept-url>/matcher configuration that maps to it) for URL-based access decisions.
The configured regular expression is written in a way whose meaning changes in the presence of line terminators (typically '.'-based wildcards such as '/admin/.*').

The underlying servlet container decodes %0d%0a (or the client can place raw CR/LF decodable into servletPath/pathInfo) so that the string returned by getServletPath()/getPathInfo() contains CR or LF.
candidates.title: RegexRequestMatcher uses unanchored full-match semantics, susceptible to line-terminator/%0d%0a request-path bypass (candidate)

counter_evidence: Within the reviewed class the destination is a method parameter with no evidence of external injection; no caller in the reviewed spans passes untrusted input.
Scheme-relative URLs such as '//evil.com' are not matched by the absolute-URL test and therefore fall into the contextPath-prefixed branch, limiting that specific bypass.
When contextRelative=true the method strips the scheme and the portion before the context path, which constrains absolute-URL use to a same-context target.
candidates.description: DefaultRedirectStrategy.sendRedirect() computes the destination via calculateRedirectUrl(request.getContextPath(), url) and then calls response.sendRedirect(redirectUrl) (lines 48-58). calculateRedirectUrl (lines 60-86) explicitly special-cases absolute URLs: when the URL is absolute and contextRelative is false it returns the URL unchanged (lines 72-74); when contextRelative is true it strips the scheme with url.substring(url.lastIndexOf("://") + 3) and then slices from the first occurrence of the context path (line 78-79). There is no allow-list, host comparison, or scheme restriction applied to the supplied URL anywhere in this class; only UrlUtils.isAbsoluteUrl(url) (line 61) is used to branch, and that check (a permissive '\A[a-z0-9.+-]+://.*' pattern) merely classifies rather than sanitizes. If a caller ever passes a user-influenced value into sendRedirect (for example a stored/redirect target), the response would be a redirect to an arbitrary absolute or scheme-relative destination. Reported as a candidate only: in the reviewed code the value is a parameter and no reviewed caller demonstrates external control, and scheme-relative ('//evil') URLs are treated as non-absolute and consequently prefixed with the context path, which reduces impact for that variant.
missing_evidence: No reviewed caller of sendRedirect was read, so untrusted reachability is not established.
The behavior of AbstractAuthenticationTargetUrlRequestHandler / SavedRequestAwareAuthenticationSuccessHandler and similar callers, which would supply the URL, was not available for inspection.
No configuration was read indicating contextRelative=true/absolute handling in any deployment.
preconditions: Some caller in the application (outside the reviewed spans) passes a request-derived or stored value (e.g. a 'target', 'redirect', 'url', or Referer-derived value) to DefaultRedirectStrategy.sendRedirect.
No separate validation of the destination is performed by that caller.
The deployment uses the default contextRelative=false setting, or a value that still resolves to an attacker-chosen host.
candidates.title: DefaultRedirectStrategy.calculateRedirectUrl returns attacker-controllable absolute/context-relative URLs without allow-list validation (candidate, precondition unproven)
